one_liner: Pure-Zig port of picohttpparser's request parser. A self-run bench claims ~1.6x over scalar picohttpparser, but the baseline was not re-measured.
what_it_does: Picozig parses an HTTP/1.x request line and headers into zero-copy slices that point into your buffer, with no allocation. The call is picozig.parseRequest(buf, *HttpRequest) -> i32 and uses picohttpparser's return convention: bytes consumed, -1 for a bad request, -2 for incomplete. It ports only phr_parse_request. There is no response parser, no headers-only parser, no chunked decoder and no last_len fast path. The package also ships an allocating HTTP response formatter and an RFC 1123 Date formatter, which are unrelated to the benchmark.
how_it_is_fast: It uses the same scalar design as picohttpparser without SSE4.2: a stateless single pass over the buffer, a 256-entry comptime lookup table for header-name token characters, and a byte-by-byte printable-ASCII scan (c -% 0x20 < 0x5F) for header values. The only 'fast' helper, findCharFast, loads 16 bytes into a @Vector(16, u8) on x86-64/aarch64 but then tests each lane in a scalar loop. It has no vector compare and no PCMPESTRI, and it is only used for the method and path tokens. The README's 'without SSE4' means no hand-written SIMD. It does not mean a no-SSE4 build: zig run targets the host CPU by default, so LLVM was free to auto-vectorize with the benchmark machine's extensions.
when_to_use: Reading or forking a compact example: about 275 lines of Zig in src/request/picozig.zig that map almost one-to-one onto picohttpparser's parse_request/parse_headers
Zig prototypes and internal services that want zero-allocation request parsing with no C in the build, where you control the clients and can hand the parser at least 100 header slots
Code that already calls picohttpparser's request API and wants the same i32 return convention in native Zig types instead of @cImport
Targets where you would build picohttpparser without SSE4.2 anyway (aarch64, other non-x86). The code is portable Zig, but no speed number exists for those targets
when_not_to_use: Internet-facing servers. The header array can overflow (see gotchas), request-line validation is looser than upstream, and there is no fuzzing or audit. The project has one contributor and 0 stars
You need responses, headers-only parsing, chunked transfer-encoding, or incremental re-parse with last_len. Only the request path is ported
You already build picohttpparser with SSE4.2 or use an AVX2 fork. The claim is only against the scalar build, and it was not measured on the same machine
Clients that send bare-LF line endings or several spaces between request-line tokens. Picozig returns -2 or -1 where picohttpparser accepts them
Anything that needs clear reuse terms. There is no license file, and the code is a translation of Perl/MIT-licensed picohttpparser without its copyright notice

integration.min_toolchain: Zig 0.15.x in practice: the last commits port it to 0.15.1, and the response helper uses the 0.15 unmanaged ArrayList API. build.zig.zon still declares minimum_zig_version 0.14.0. Not verified on Zig 0.16.0 (released 2026-04-13)
integration.platforms: Any Zig target: pure Zig with no intrinsics and no syscalls in the parser. findCharFast uses 16-byte vectors on x86-64/aarch64 and 8-byte vectors elsewhere. Benchmarked only on x86-64 (AMD Ryzen 8845H)
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. From the source, parseRequest is stateless and writes only to the caller's HttpRequest and header array, so concurrent calls with separate outputs look safe
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — it mirrors phr_parse_request's return codes and zero-copy output, but it is a Zig API with no C ABI. phr_parse_response, phr_parse_headers, phr_decode_chunked and the last_len argument are missing. It also ignores the caller's num_headers capacity

gotchas: Header-array overflow: parseRequest ignores params.num_headers and slices the many-item pointer as headers[0..100]. A request with more headers than your array writes past its end, and Zig cannot bounds-check a [*]T slice in any build mode. The repo's own bench and a zig-httpuring test pass 32 slots, and test.zig passes 4-14. Always supply at least 100

Looser than picohttpparser on the request line. test.zig asserts success for an empty method (' / HTTP/1.0') and an empty target ('GET  HTTP/1.0'), where upstream test.c expects -1. The method is not checked against token characters, so ':GET' is accepted. Multiple spaces between tokens, which upstream accepts, are rejected

Header values keep trailing spaces and tabs (upstream trims them). A request whose final empty line is a lone LF at the end of the buffer returns -2 (incomplete) until more bytes arrive. test.zig asserts this for 'GET / HTTP/1.0
Host: example.com

'

HttpRequest.body is never filled in. Errors come back only as i32 codes, because the internal ParseError is not surfaced. The bundled response formatter heap-allocates a StringHashMap and an ArrayList for every response
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Among the Zig siblings, hparse also beats picohttpparser and reports wall time, cycles and instructions against it, which makes it the better-evidenced choice. Picozig is mainly worth picking as a minimal, readable scalar translation of pico's request path to study or fork. For production use, the vkrasnov AVX2 fork, httparse or httpp (about 2.26x at -O3) have stronger benchmark evidence and more complete APIs.
verified_claims_summary: src/request/bench.zig parses picohttpparser's bench.c 'kittyhell' request (10 headers, 32-slot array) 10 million times in one run, timed with a millisecond wall clock. Built with zig run -O ReleaseFast (Zig version not stated; the code targets 0.15.1) for the native CPU, it printed 5,086,000 requests/s on an AMD Ryzen 8845H mobile CPU. The '~3.2M headers/sec without SSE4' picohttpparser figure has no stated source and was not re-measured: upstream bench.c has no timer and was not run on that machine. The units also differ, so the ~1.6x is only indicative.
status_note: Counts as active under the 12-month rule (last commit 2025-10-11, a port to Zig 0.15.1). In practice it is a 9-commit, single-author, unlicensed side project that only the author's own repos use (zig-httpuring and buddy-blocks, via a relative ../zig-pico path), so treat it as reference code rather than a dependency.
